_doc: D103: every five floors a lead finds something in the Tower that gives a chapter of who they were back (D53). Each memory is a found object: `area` and `cell` say where it lies (on the way to the stair, and the compass points at it first, D107), `art` the prop drawn there (a stand-in until art request A10 is made), `scene` the lines played when it is picked up, and `journal` the line written into the journal's Quests page. Only the lead it belongs to finds it. Read by src/chronicle/memories.gd. Atlas's chapter one is the meeting 2 draft; Cato's (the quiz's most common second lead) is the 2026-10-15 draft Will kept, in the same alcove, which only he finds; Janus, Bellona, Cassius, Saturn, Pluto, Ultor and Liber, the leads with enough founder material (Will, 2026-10-15), lie there too (D138), and so do Ares, Caesar, Vesta, Iris, Ceres, Juno and Diana, drafted from Will's three inspiration volumes and rewritten by the creatives' meeting (D151), so all sixteen have one; the working draft (call F); **Inferred** and the founders' to rewrite; the faces stay blank while CH10 is open. Chapter two (D254, the Second Hour) lies on floors 6 to 10, one keepsake a lead, written from the chapter-two drafts by tools/chapter_twos.py; **Inferred** too.

atlas.title: Chapter one: The Weight

scene.text: Half under the dust by the wall: a buckle, small enough for a child's saddle, the leather long gone from it.
Atlas closes his hand on it, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A courtyard of white stone, before the fall. The others are playing a running game. He cannot run. He is sitting where he was put.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: They gave you the long road because you're the only one of us who'll see what's at the end of it. Don't let them tell you that's a punishment.
He turns to find who is speaking. There is a shape against the light, and no more.
Something pushes under his hand: a lizard the size of a dog, too heavy for its own legs, looking up at him as if he were the only thing in the courtyard.
White.
The fifth floor again, cold under him, the buckle in his fist and Sky's head under his other hand. Sky was given, not found. Somebody up there meant him to be carried, and meant him to arrive.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Weight.

atlas.journal: Floor 5. I remembered a white courtyard and a voice, and that Sky was a gift, though not who gave him.

atlas.title: Chapter two: The Last Page

scene.text: Pinned under a loose stone on the landing: the torn corner of a page, the ink gone brown, one word left on it. _Carried._
Atlas reads it before he means to, the way he reads everything, and the floor goes out from under the world.

Lamplight on shelves that climb out of sight, white stone to the ceiling, before the fall. He is small enough to sit in the reading chair with his feet off the floor. Someone is reading to him from a very old book.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Sixteen go down. Some climb back. At the top they are made to fight each other, until one is left. That's the end. That's always been the end.

scene.speaker: Atlas
scene.text: Then I'll go. Somebody should know the ending, and still be there when it comes.
The voice closes the book and does not argue, as if it knew he would say it. Above the hands on the cover there is only lamplight.
White.
On the sixth floor, the scrap still in his fist, Atlas has it at last. He was not sent down. He asked to go, because he had read to the last page, and he went to change it.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Last Page.

atlas.journal: Floor 6. I read the old book to its end, where the sixteen who climb are set against each other at the top, and I asked to go down anyway.

cato.title: Chapter one: The Last Line

scene.text: Wedged in a crack at the foot of the alcove wall: a bronze stylus, the kind for writing on wax, its point worn flat with use.
Cato turns it over once, the way he checks a blade for a nick, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A lamp burnt low on a desk of white stone, before the fall. He is writing on a wax tablet and has been for hours. At the top, in his own hand: IF IT GOES WRONG.
One. Find the others. Two. Trust nobody who cannot tell you the rules. He has filled the tablet to its last line.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: You've written down every way this ends badly. Where's the line for what we do if it works?

scene.speaker: Cato
scene.text: If it works, nobody needs a list.
The voice laughs, and a thumb smooths the wax over his last line before he can read it back. He tries to see whose hand it is. The face will not come.
White.

Cato wakes on the fifth floor with the stylus in his fist and knows one thing he did not know before: the fall did not take him by surprise. He saw it coming and wrote the rules for it, and somebody he trusted rubbed one out.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Last Line.

cato.journal: Floor 5. I remembered a list I wrote for if it went wrong. The first rule was find the others. Somebody wiped the last one before I could read it.

cato.title: Chapter two: The Roll
cato.object: a wax tablet's frame, a line scored in the wood

scene.text: Face-down on the bench by the keeper's door: the frame of a wax tablet, the wax long gone. Something is scored into the bare wood where a stylus once went through.
Cato reads it with his thumb, as he would a seal, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Inside a wall of white stone, the night it held, before the fall. Cato sits at a table by the gate with a lamp and the roll, writing down every name that comes in off the road.
A whistle. The gate comes down. And under it, last, on his belly, a boy with a knife in his teeth. Not on any roll.
Cato writes him in at the bottom, as the boy says it: _Ultor. Came in under the gate. Will not forgive it._

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Leave that one off. Let him be nobody. Nobody hunts a nobody.

scene.speaker: Cato
scene.text: Everyone goes on the roll. That's what a roll is for.
The voice takes the tablet from him, gently, and he lets it. He looks up to put a name to the hand. The lamp has burnt too low.
White.
The tenth floor, and the frame in his fist. He wrote Ultor's name down before he ever hunted him. Somebody he trusted wanted that boy forgotten, to keep him safe, and Cato would not leave him off.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Roll.

cato.journal: Floor 10. The night the gate held, I put the last one in on the roll, a boy called Ultor, though someone wanted him left off.

janus.title: Chapter one: The Shut Door

scene.text: Lying across the alcove's threshold as if it fell out of a door that is no longer there: an iron hinge pin, as long as a finger, rust on its head.
Janus picks it up only because it is in his way, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A hall of white stone, before the fall, and at the end of it a door that will not open. Everyone has tried it. Janus is asleep against it, his back to the wood.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: You could open it. Everyone here knows you could. You just don't want to.

scene.speaker: Janus
scene.text: If I open it, it stops being interesting.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Then promise me one thing. When a door opens that nobody can explain, you get up. Whatever it costs. You get up and you go through.
He says yes, mostly so the voice will let him sleep, and does not open his eyes to see who asked. Now he cannot.
White.

Janus comes to on the fifth floor with the pin in his fist and lies there, working it out. It was never the gates that got him up. It was a promise, made to somebody, and he meant it more than he let them see.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Shut Door.

janus.journal: Floor 5. I slept against a shut door once and promised somebody I would get up for the hard ones, and I cannot think who.

janus.title: Chapter two: The Other Side
janus.object: a blank key with no teeth

scene.text: Balanced on the sill of the one doorway nobody bricked up: a key with no teeth, never cut, the bow worn smooth by somebody's thumb.
Janus tries it in the air, in no lock at all, and the floor goes out from under the world.
The shut door from before, the night after he promised, and for once he is awake. He opens it. It was never locked; it was only heavy.
Behind it is a round room of white stone with sixteen more doors in its wall, every one shut, every one humming like a hive.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: One for each of you. Each one stays shut while its keeper lives. When one dies, theirs opens, and everything behind it can come through.

scene.speaker: Janus
scene.text: And this room? Whose is this?

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Nobody's. That's why I'm giving it to you.
The voice puts a blank key in his hand and leaves him there. By the time he thinks to turn round, the doorway is empty.
White.
The eighth floor, and the key in his fist. So the gates down here are those doors, and the room between them is his. The promise was never only to get up. It was to keep watch on them.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Other Side.

janus.journal: Floor 8. Behind the door were sixteen more, one for each of us and shut until its keeper dies, and somebody gave me the room between them and a key that fits nothing yet.

bellona.title: Chapter one: The Order

scene.text: Caught on a nail at the back of the alcove, swinging a little though there is no wind: a bronze signal whistle on a cut cord, dented flat on one side.
Bellona takes it down the way she would take a report, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A gate in a wall of white stone, before the fall, and night outside it. Something is coming up the road, fast and too many. She is on the wall, and the whistle is in her teeth.
There are still people on the road. Not many. Running.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: They'll make it. Give them to the count of twenty.

scene.speaker: Bellona
scene.text: We don't have twenty. Shut it.
She blows the whistle, and the gate comes down, and she does not look over the wall. She never turns to see who asked for twenty.
White.

Bellona is on her feet on the fifth floor before she is properly awake, the whistle in her fist. She has given that order before, once, above. The fear was never of giving it. It was of being the one who can.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Order.

bellona.journal: Floor 5. I shut a gate on people still running for it, and I would do it again, but I do not know who was outside.

bellona.title: Chapter two: The Count of Twenty
bellona.object: the snapped point of Ultor's knife

scene.text: Wedged in the top step of the broken stair, as if it struck there and stayed: the point of a knife, a thumb's width of steel, bent.
Bellona works it free with a thumbnail, and knows where it was aimed before she knows why, and the floor goes out from under the world.
The same wall, an hour after the gate came down, before the fall. The road outside has gone quiet. She stands where she gave the order and counts to twenty, slowly, where nobody can hear.
Something comes up the wall stair fast and low. A boy, with a knife. It goes for her throat, cuts the whistle's cord, and snaps on the mail at her collar.
Her soldiers have him down in a breath. One asks his name, with a boot on his back. "Ultor," he says, into the stone. "Remember it."

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: He came at the commander. You know what the order is.

scene.speaker: Bellona
scene.text: Let him go. He's earned one.
They let him go. She looks along the wall for whoever quoted her own orders at her, and cannot pick them out among the helmets.
White.
The seventh floor, and the steel in her fist. The boy from the road is called Ultor, and she let him go. He will come again. She knew that when she gave the order, and gave it anyway.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Count of Twenty.

bellona.journal: Floor 7. A boy called Ultor came up the wall stair for me and broke his knife on my mail, and I let him go.

cassius.title: Chapter one: The Mask

scene.text: Face-down in the dust of the alcove: a child's festival mask, a monster's face in painted clay, cracked from brow to chin.
Cassius turns it over, and the face grins up at him as if it knows him, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A festival in a square of white stone, before the fall. The children are playing heroes and monsters. There is one monster's mask, and nobody will wear it, so they are making the smallest one.
He takes the mask out of the small one's hands and puts it on himself.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Why would you want to be the monster?

scene.speaker: Cassius
scene.text: Somebody has to be. Better someone who can argue back.
The voice laughs, not unkindly, and says they will remember him in it. He looks out through the eyeholes for whoever said it. The holes are too small.
White.
On the fifth floor the mask is still grinning in his fist. Nobody ever made Cassius the monster. He asked for it, to spare somebody smaller, and he would ask again.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Mask.

cassius.journal: Floor 5. Nobody made me the monster at the festival; I took the mask out of a smaller child's hands and asked for it.

cassius.title: Chapter two: The Hand

scene.text: Caught under the broken leg of a market stall: a winner's ribbon, blue once, trodden flat, a heel-print still on it.
Cassius picks it up by one end, as if it might bite, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Behind the stalls, after the game, before the fall. He sits in the dust with the cracked mask in his lap. Out in the square, they are still cheering.
The hero comes round the stalls alone, with the crown still on, and holds out his hand. Cassius looks at it and does not take it.
The smallest child, the one he took the mask from, crouches beside him when the hero has gone and pushes the ribbon into his hand. "They threw it for Caesar. I picked it up for you."

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: He meant it, you know, the hand. Caesar means everything he does. That's what you can't forgive him.

scene.speaker: Cassius
scene.text: I can forgive him anything. It's them I can't.
He nods at the noise. Whoever knows him that well is standing just behind him, and he will not give them the satisfaction of looking round.
White.

Cassius wakes on the eighth floor with the ribbon wound round his fingers. The hero was Caesar. He held out his hand, and Cassius left it hanging. He has argued it both ways since, principle and pride, and won neither.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Hand.

cassius.journal: Floor 8. The hero was called Caesar, and I would not take his hand, so a child gave me the ribbon they threw for him.

saturn.title: Chapter one: The Mended Bowl

scene.text: Set upright in the middle of the alcove, as if someone had put it down for a guest: a small clay bowl, cracked in three and mended with black pitch.
Saturn lifts it in both hands, the way you take something offered, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A long table of white stone, before the fall, laid for a meal. He laid it. He has set a place for everyone, and he is waiting, and one place stays empty.
The bowl at that place is this one, before it was broken.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: They're not coming. You know they're not. You can't keep a place for everyone.

scene.speaker: Saturn
scene.text: Then I'll keep it for the ones nobody else will.
He fills the empty bowl anyway, and it cracks in his hands. Across the table, where a face should be, there is only the chair.
White.

Saturn wakes on the fifth floor holding the bowl as you hold a thing that has broken once. The loss did not start here. He brought it down with him. Somebody above did not come back, and he has set their place ever since.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Mended Bowl.

saturn.journal: Floor 5. I laid a table for everyone once and one place stayed empty, and I still set it, though I cannot remember whose it is.

saturn.title: Chapter two: The Easy Way Up

scene.text: Set neatly at the foot of the last stair, as if somebody stepped out of it and went on: one sandal, worn thin, its strap still buckled.
Saturn kneels to put it straight, as he would for a guest, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Dawn on a rooftop, before the fall, and above it a light that is not the sun, coming down like a ladder. People are climbing it. Nobody climbs it carrying anything.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: There's a way up that doesn't hurt. They've promised. You don't have to earn it. Come with me.

scene.speaker: Saturn
scene.text: When everyone can come, I'll come. Not before.
The one he loves goes up the light, and steps out of a sandal on the way, and does not look down. Nobody who climbs it is ever seen again. At the top the light is too bright to make them out.
He goes down and lays the table, and keeps their place.
White.

On the tenth floor Saturn sets the sandal down beside him, straight. The empty place is theirs, and the easy way up was a lie. Somebody up there sells an ascension that is not one. They will answer for it.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Easy Way Up.

saturn.journal: Floor 10. The one I loved climbed a light like a ladder without me, and nobody came back down, because it was never heaven and somebody lied to them.

pluto.title: Chapter one: The Tally

scene.text: Leaning in the corner of the alcove: a tally stick of black wood, notched along both edges and down one face, no room left for another mark.
Pluto runs his thumb down the notches, counting without meaning to, and the floor goes out from under the world.
The top of a stair of white stone, before the fall, and nothing above it but sky. He is standing there. He got there first. He is alone.
He is counting the ones who started the climb with him. Every notch is one of them. None of them is on the stair.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: You did it. You're at the top. Was it worth what it cost them?

scene.speaker: Pluto
scene.text: Next time, nobody pays it but me.
He means it the way he means a ledger. He does not look round at who asked. He is still counting.
White.

Pluto wakes on the fifth floor with the stick in his fist and the count unfinished. He was right: he has been at the top. He got there alone, over everyone who climbed with him, and it was not worth it.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Tally.

pluto.journal: Floor 5. I stood alone at the top of the stair, counting the ones who climbed with me, and this time nobody pays for it but me.

pluto.title: Chapter two: The Rounds
pluto.object: a black stone token, one notch

scene.text: On the top step, where a winner would stand: a token of black stone the size of a coin, a single notch cut into it.
Pluto weighs it, the way he weighs everything, and the floor goes out from under the world.
The foot of the stair, this time, before the fall, and a crowd all round it, high up on benches, too far off to see. The ones who will climb are standing in a line. He knows every one of them.
Every hundred steps the climb stops, and two of them are set against each other, and only one goes on. He goes on, every time.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: You can stop. Lose one. Nobody would know you meant it.

scene.speaker: Pluto
scene.text: They'd know. And they'd only have to fight someone worse.
He wins the last round at the top and is given the token, and the crowd is already leaving. The one who said he could stop has gone with them.
White.

Pluto wakes on the tenth floor with the token's one notch under his thumb. The top was a contest, and every notch on the tally was someone he beat on the way up. Somebody means to hold another. This time Pluto ends it.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Rounds.

pluto.journal: Floor 10. The stair was a contest and every notch on my tally someone I beat, and there is going to be another one.

ultor.title: Chapter one: The Wrong Side
ultor.object: a knife hilt with no blade

scene.text: Driven into the floor of the alcove up to the guard, as if somebody meant it to stay: the hilt of a knife, its blade snapped off a thumb's width from the guard.
Ultor works it loose, and the floor goes out from under the world.

A road at night, before the fall, running up to a gate in a wall of white stone. Something is behind them, fast and too many. He is running, and somebody's hand is on his collar, dragging him, because he is small and slow.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Twenty more strides. They'll hold it for us. Run.
A whistle on the wall. The gate comes down.
The hand lets go of his collar and shoves him into the gap under the closing gate, and the one it belongs to stays on the road. He twists round to see their face, and the gate is in the way.
He only hears the whistle, again and again, all the way down.
White.
Ultor wakes on the fifth floor with the hilt in his fist. It was never a face he hated. It was whoever blew that whistle. The one he would have followed anywhere died on the wrong side of it.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Wrong Side.

ultor.journal: Floor 5. Someone shoved me under a closing gate and stayed on the road, and I don't have their face, but I'll know the whistle.

ultor.title: Chapter two: The Name

scene.text: Under the rubble at the foot of the stair: a short length of cord, cut through, a knot at one end where something hung.
Ultor knows the cut, because he made it, and the floor goes out from under the world.

An hour after the gate, inside it, before the fall. Somebody at a table by the gate is writing his name down; he can hear the stylus scratch. He takes the knife from his teeth and goes looking for the whistle.
He finds it on the wall, at a throat. He cuts the cord. The blade breaks on the mail beneath, a thumb's width from the guard.
They have him on the stone before the whistle hits the ground. A boot on his back. Somebody shouts for the commander by name: "Bellona!"

scene.speaker: Bellona
scene.text: Let him go. He's earned one.
Nobody has ever let him go before. He does not thank her. He tries to look up at her, and the boot on his back keeps his face in the stone.
White.
Ultor wakes on the seventh floor winding the cord round two fingers. The whistle has a name now: Bellona. She let him live, once. That is worse than anything else she could have done to him.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Name.

ultor.journal: Floor 7. I cut the whistle from her throat and broke my knife on her mail, and they called her Bellona, and she let me go.

liber.title: Chapter one: The Cut Rope

scene.text: Knotted round a ring in the alcove wall, the rest of it lying on the floor: a length of rope, cut clean through, its knot still tied.
Liber laughs at it, because a rope that has already been cut is the best kind, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A yard of white stone at night, before the fall. He is small, and the yard gate is tied shut, and on the other side of it is everything.
He saws at the rope with a stone until his hands bleed. It parts. The gate opens a crack.
Someone big is standing in the yard behind him. The one who teaches him to fight with a wooden sword, and lets him win. He has seen everything.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Go on, then. Go. I'll say I left it open.
Liber goes, and does not look back, and is happy the whole way down the road. He never looked back, so he has no face to remember.
White.
Liber wakes on the fifth floor grinning, the rope in his fist, and then stops grinning. Somebody set him free once, and paid for it, and never told him. He would very much like to say thank you.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Cut Rope.

liber.journal: Floor 5. I cut the rope on a gate and ran, and someone took the blame for it, and I mean to find them and say thank you.

liber.title: Chapter two: The Wraps

scene.text: Hanging from the windlass of a dry well: a strip of linen wound for a small fist, stiff and brown with old blood, still the shape of a hand.
Liber slips his fingers into it, and it nearly fits, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Noon in the yard, before the fall, and he has been hitting the wooden sword with his bare hands until they split. The big one is laughing so hard he has to sit down.
The big one winds linen round the small split fists, slowly, one and then the other.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Ares! Bring the little one in, it's time!
He does not move. He finishes the second hand first.

scene.speaker: Ares
scene.text: Hands are for holding on, Liber. Fists are for when you have to. Don't get them mixed up.
Then he lets Liber knock him down with the sword, and lies in the dust pretending it hurt. Whoever called them in is only a voice from a doorway, and the doorway stays dark.
White.
Liber wakes on the ninth floor with the wraps still on his hand, and leaves them there. The big one is Ares, and Ares is family. He is somewhere down here too, and Liber owes him a thank you.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Wraps.

liber.journal: Floor 9. The big one who wrapped my hands and let me go is Ares, my family, and I'm going to find him and thank him properly.

ares.title: Chapter one: The One He Let Go

scene.text: Propped in the corner of the alcove as if somebody meant to come back for it: a child's wooden sword, notched all down one edge.
Ares laughs at the size of it, picks it up, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Before the fall, in a yard of white stone, he is teaching someone small to fight with this sword, and losing on purpose, and laughing. The small one is quick and does not stay where he is put.
That night he finds the yard gate's rope cut through, a stone beside it, wet. The gate stands open a crack. He saw the small one go, and said nothing.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: The yard gate was open all night. Who left it open?

scene.speaker: Ares
scene.text: Me. Forgot. Put it on my name.
He takes the punishment, and he is glad the whole time. He tries to call up the small one's face, and gets only a back, running.
White.

Ares wakes on the fifth floor laughing, the little sword in his fist. He has let someone go before, and lied for it, and never once been sorry. Whoever sends him after outlaws had better not send him after that one.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The One He Let Go.

ares.journal: Floor 5. I taught someone small to fight and lied for him when he cut the yard gate's rope, and I was glad to, whoever he was.

ares.title: Chapter two: Put It on My Name

scene.text: Looped over the post in the middle of the yard: one link of iron chain, worn bright on the inside where it rubbed.
Ares rubs his wrist without meaning to, laughs at himself, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Morning, before the fall, in the same yard. He is chained to the post with his arms up and has been all night. His back is open. The rope on the yard gate has been mended.
Someone stands in front of him with the cut end of that rope in their hand.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Say it was Liber. Say his name, and you come down, and we send riders after him.

scene.speaker: Ares
scene.text: Liber? Never heard of him. HA! I forgot the gate. Put it on my name.
They put it on his name, and it costs him the day, and the next, and he laughs through all of it. He keeps his eyes on the gate, never on the one holding the rope.
White.
Ares wakes on the ninth floor and rubs his wrist again. The small one was Liber, his own kin, and Ares had the name the whole time they were asking for it. Let them ask again.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, Put It on My Name.

ares.journal: Floor 9. They chained me to the post and asked me for Liber's name, and I said I'd never heard of him, and I'd say it again.

caesar.title: Chapter one: The Hero's Part

scene.text: Lying in the dust of the alcove, bent nearly flat as if someone had stood on it: a child's crown cut from tin, a few flecks of gold paint still on it.
Caesar bends it back into a circle without thinking, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Noon, before the fall, and the square of white stone is full for the festival. The children are playing heroes and monsters, and he is the hero. He has the crown. Everyone is cheering for him.
He wins, of course. The monster goes down in the dust, mask and all, and the square roars his name.
Afterwards he finds the monster sitting alone behind the stalls, the mask cracked across. He holds out his hand. It is not taken.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Don't worry about that one. Somebody has to lose. You were wonderful.
He wants to ask who was under the mask, and he does not, and the crowd carries him off. Over their heads he looks back for the monster's face, and sees only the mask.
White.
Caesar wakes on the fifth floor with the crown bent round in his fist. For every cheer he ever had, somebody stood in the dust, and he never once asked who. He will ask now.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Hero's Part.

caesar.journal: Floor 5. I played the hero at a festival and everyone cheered, and someone played the monster so I could, and I never asked who.

caesar.title: Chapter two: Who Was Under It
caesar.object: a red clay horn from the mask

scene.text: In the gutter by the dry fountain: a chip of painted clay, a horn, faded red, broken off a mask.
Caesar turns it over, looking for the rest of the face, and the floor goes out from under the world.

Evening, before the fall, and the festival packed away. He has come back to the square alone. The crown is in his pocket. The monster's mask lies in the dust where it was dropped, a horn knocked off it.
He asks everyone who is left who wore it. Nobody knows. Then the smallest child says, as if it were obvious: "Cassius. He took it so I wouldn't have to."

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Leave it. You were the hero. That's a good thing to have been.

scene.speaker: Caesar
scene.text: Then I'll go and tell him he was the best monster I ever fought! He'll cheer up. Everyone does.
He knocks at Cassius's door until dark. It does not open. The one who told him to leave it has gone, and he never thought to look at them.
White.
On the eighth floor Caesar sits up with the horn in his fist. The monster was Cassius, who took the mask so somebody smaller would not have to. The door never opened. Caesar is still knocking.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, Who Was Under It.

caesar.journal: Floor 8. The monster was Cassius, who took the mask for a little one, and he would not open his door to me, so I'll find him.

vesta.title: Chapter one: The One Who Stayed

scene.text: On a ledge in the alcove, as if someone set it there and meant to come back: a small clay lamp, its wick burnt down to nothing. It is still warm.
Vesta closes her hand round it, and the floor goes out from under the world.

The last fire in a house of white stone, before the fall, and the house emptying. She is kneeling at the hearth. Across the room a doorway stands full of light, and everyone is walking into it. On the other side is how things were, before it all went wrong.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Come with us. It's better there. It was always better there. Nobody has to stay.

scene.speaker: Vesta
scene.text: Then who keeps this one?
They go. Every one of them. She lights the lamp from the hearth, and keeps them both going in the empty house, and does not cry where anyone could see.
The one who asked her last stood in the doorway, and the light behind them took the face with it.
White.
Vesta wakes on the fifth floor with the lamp still warm in her hands. She has been offered the way back once already. She said no, and they left her alone for it. She would say no again.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The One Who Stayed.

vesta.journal: Floor 5. Everyone went through the door back to how things were, and I stayed and kept the fire, and I still would.

vesta.title: Chapter two: The One Who Came Back

scene.text: Under the ash in a cold chimney corner: a lump of hearthstone, white on one face and burnt black on the other. It is warm.
Vesta holds it to her cheek before she can think better of it, and the floor goes out from under the world.

Winter in the empty house, before the fall, months after they all went. The fire is low and she is feeding it one stick at a time. Someone is standing in the room with her, thin, smiling the old smile.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: It isn't how it was, over there. It's how we wanted it. It never ends. Come anyway. Please.

scene.speaker: Vesta
scene.text: You're cold. Come to the fire.
They come closer to the fire, and the light goes through them, and they are not there; only ash on the hearth, settling. The face goes first.
She sweeps the ash into the hearth and keeps the fire going, and does not cry where anyone could see.
White.
On the ninth floor the stone is still warm against her cheek. The way back is the dead wearing better days. Her fire was never only for her. It shows them for what they are.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The One Who Came Back.

vesta.journal: Floor 9. One of them came back to ask me again, and my fire went through them, and the way back was only dying, dressed up.

iris.title: Chapter one: The Pass

scene.text: Rolled into the corner of the alcove, as if kicked there long ago: a small stitched leather ball, half flat, scuffed pale on one side.
Iris taps it up onto her foot before she can stop herself, and the floor goes out from under the world.
One moment left in a game that matters more than a game should, played on white stone before the fall. The ball is at her feet and there is nobody between her and the mark.
She sees someone else open, out wide, and passes. They miss, and the courtyard goes loud, not for her side.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: You had it. You had it, and you gave it away. Why?

scene.speaker: Iris
scene.text: Because they were open too.
The voice does not argue. It only says: so were you. She is already running back up the pitch, and never sees who said it.
White.
Iris wakes on the fifth floor with the ball under her foot. So the flinch has a name. Once, when it mattered most, the shot was hers, and she gave it away. Next time she takes it.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Pass.

iris.journal: Floor 5. The shot was mine in the last moment of the game, and I passed, and we lost, and next time I take it.

iris.title: Chapter two: The First Rumour

scene.text: Tied round a pillar at shoulder height, at the far end of the gallery: a yellow armband, knotted where it was torn from a sleeve.
Iris unties it with her teeth, quick, the way she does everything, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Dusk against the courtyard wall, the same evening, before the fall. The one she passed to, the one who missed, is sitting against the wall with their colours torn off, and nobody will go near them.
Iris sits down beside them. Neither of them says anything for a long time.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Everyone's saying it was their miss. You could tell them you passed. You could tell them the truth.

scene.speaker: Iris
scene.text: I'll tell them I slipped. They'll believe me. They always believe me.
By morning everyone knows Iris slipped. It is the first story she ever started. Whoever asked her for the truth is lost in the telling.
White.

Iris is up off the sixth floor before she has properly woken, the armband in her fist. Her first rumour was a lie to cover somebody else. She has carried everyone's news since, so she never has to carry her own.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The First Rumour.

iris.journal: Floor 6. Everyone blamed the one I passed to for the miss, so I told them I slipped, and that was the first rumour I ever started.

ceres.title: Chapter one: The Last Sheaf

scene.text: Somebody has tucked a corn dolly into a crack in the alcove wall, plaited from the last sheaf of some harvest, gone grey with years.
Ceres knows the plait before she touches it, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Harvest, before the fall, and a granary of white stone full to the rafters. A dozen children are hidden in the grain, none of them hers. Out in the fields, in the dark, something is walking.
It stops at the granary wall. She can hear it breathing. She is not strong, and there is nowhere else to put them.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: You can't hide all of them.

scene.speaker: Ceres
scene.text: Watch me.
She lifts the last child into the grain pit, sits down on its lid, and does not get up until morning. She never looks round to see who said she couldn't.
White.

Ceres wakes on the fifth floor with the dolly in her fist. The village is not the first harvest she has hidden children in. She never learnt how many were alive at sunrise. This time she will count every one.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Last Sheaf.

ceres.journal: Floor 5. I sat all night on a pit lid over children who weren't mine while something walked the fields, and I don't know how many I kept, but this time I'll keep them all.

ceres.title: Chapter two: The Thirteenth
ceres.object: a tiny shoe full of grain

scene.text: Upright at the bottom of the dry cistern: a child's shoe, very small, full to the top with grain.
Ceres tips the grain out into her palm to see if it is good, and the floor goes out from under the world.
Grey light, before the fall, before sunrise. She gets up off the pit lid with legs gone dead under her and starts lifting them out of the grain by feel, one at a time, saying each name.
She stops at a hand she does not know. Small, cold, holding on to hers very hard. Nobody answers to it.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: That isn't one of them. You know it isn't. Put it back.

scene.speaker: Ceres
scene.text: Then it's one of mine now. I've fed stranger.
She lifts it out with the others and does not look at it until it is in the sun. She does not look at the one who told her to put it back, either.
White.

Ceres wakes on the seventh floor and pours the grain back into the shoe, every seed. One in the pit was never hers, and she kept it with the rest. She still does not know how many of hers came out. That one did.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Thirteenth.

ceres.journal: Floor 7. Lifting them out of the grain at dawn I found a hand I didn't know, and kept that one too, and I still don't know how many of mine there were.

juno.title: Chapter one: The Last Plate

scene.text: Hung on a hook in the alcove wall, where a kitchen would keep it: a wooden spoon, cracked, its bowl burnt black.
Juno takes it down and checks the crack with her thumb, and the floor goes out from under the world.
A great house of white stone, before the fall. She is small, and shut in a cold room for crying when she should not have. Nobody has brought her anything for a long time.
The door opens a crack. Someone old, with flour on his sleeves, puts down a plate: the last of the stew, scraped from the pot with this spoon.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Eat. Go on. I've had mine.
He had not. She knows it by how thin he is, and eats anyway, because he wants her to. His face is behind the steam, and the steam does not clear.
She promises him, with her mouth full: nobody at her table will ever go without.
White.
Juno wakes on the fifth floor with the spoon in her fist, the crack under her thumb. Somebody went hungry so she could eat, and never said so. Every table she has laid since is her paying it back.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Last Plate.

juno.journal: Floor 5. An old cook gave me the last of the pot and said he'd eaten, and he hadn't, so nobody at my table goes hungry.

juno.title: Chapter two: The Back Door

scene.text: Hanging from the last hook in the empty storeroom: a cook's apron string, knotted twice round nothing, as if the waist it was tied on has gone.
Juno unpicks the knot because she cannot bear a bad knot, and the floor goes out from under the world.

Snow in the kitchen yard of the great house, years on, before the fall. She is grown. The old cook stands in it with his bundle, sent out for feeding a child who was being punished. Everyone knows which child.
Nobody in the house will look at him. Juno comes out the back with a plate, the first she ever cooked, and puts it in his hands.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Go back in, girl. They'll take it out on you. You've a place here. I haven't.

scene.speaker: Juno
scene.text: Then I haven't either. Eat. Go on. I've had mine.
She had not. He knows it by the look of her and eats anyway, because she wants him to. The snow is between them, and it will not stop falling.
White.

On the sixth floor Juno ties the apron string round her own waist, properly. She was not sent from the great house. She walked out after him with a plate and never went back. Every inn she has kept is that back door.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Back Door.

juno.journal: Floor 6. They turned the old cook out in the snow for feeding me, so I went after him with a plate and never went back in.

diana.title: Chapter one: The Collar

scene.text: Hanging from a stone in the alcove wall, as if left for whoever would need it: a leather collar, frayed, far too big for any dog.
Diana lifts it down very carefully, as if it might wake, and the floor goes out from under the world.

Up on a hill, before the fall, where the stone is white and warm, she sits with the wolf asleep beside her. It is bigger than she remembered. The village below leaves offerings at the hill's foot, and is afraid of the hill. She is afraid of them.
Lanterns at the foot of the hill, and somebody calling up it, not coming one step nearer.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: We've brought the offerings, lady. Keep it fed. Keep it up there.

scene.speaker: Diana
scene.text: They think it's me.
She says it to the wolf, quietly, not to them. The wolf only puts its head on her knee and stays. The one calling is a lantern at the foot of the hill, and she does not go down to see more.
White.

Diana wakes on the fifth floor with the collar held against her. The wolf could have gone down the hill any night it liked. It stayed, and let them fear her, so nobody would climb up and find how frightened she was.
A new page in the journal: Chapter one, The Collar.

diana.journal: Floor 5. The wolf could have gone down the hill any night, and it stayed and let the village think the danger was me, to keep them away from me.

diana.title: Chapter two: The Trap

scene.text: Half buried among the roots of the dead tree: a small iron trap, rusted, its jaws pried open and bent back.
Diana goes very still, the way she does when the wolf goes still, and the floor goes out from under the world.
The hill's foot in winter, years before the hill was hers, before the fall. She is small, and alone, and something in the snow is screaming. A wolf cub, its foreleg in a trap.
A man from the village comes down the path with a club, not hurrying.

scene.speaker: A voice
scene.text: Leave it, girl. It'll grow up and come for us. They always do.

scene.speaker: Diana
scene.text: Then it can come for me first.
She opens the jaws with her hands, and they cut her, and she does not let go until the cub is out. The man does not come one step nearer. She never looks up from the cub to see his face.
White.

Diana wakes on the ninth floor with the trap in her lap, and looks at her palms. She was not always the frightened one. Once she went down the hill alone and put her hands in iron, and the wolf has repaid it since.
A new page in the journal: Chapter two, The Trap.

diana.journal: Floor 9. I opened a trap on a wolf cub with my bare hands while a man with a club watched, and I was small, and I was not afraid.
